Advanced Statistical Learning for Physiological Stress Prediction

Jenna Lu

2026-07-27

Overview

Predicting physiological stress requires models capable of identifying complex patterns in cardiovascular signals while remaining interpretable and statistically rigorous.

Previous notebooks introduced preprocessing, feature engineering, Bayesian modeling, mixed-effects models, and machine learning using heart rate data. This notebook synthesizes those analyses by comparing multiple statistical learning methods for stress classification across the WESAD dataset.

Objectives:

  1. Engineer informative heart rate features
  2. Explore feature relationships
  3. Visualize physiological structure using PCA
  4. Compare multiple statistical learning algorithms
  5. Evaluate predictive performance

Libraries

library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(pROC)
library(MASS)
library(class)
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(brms)

Load Heart Rate Files

# Load Heart Rate Files

hr_files <- list.files(
  here("data","processed"),
  pattern="_heart_rate.csv$",
  full.names=TRUE
)


hr_all <- purrr::map_dfr(
  hr_files,
  function(file){

    subject <- stringr::str_extract(
      basename(file),
      "S[0-9]+"
    )

    read_csv(
      file,
      show_col_types = FALSE
    ) %>%
      mutate(
        subject = subject
      )

  }
)


glimpse(hr_all)

Load Condition Labels

condition_files <- list.files(
  here("data","processed"),
  pattern="_ecg_filtered.csv$",
  full.names=TRUE
)


condition_all <- purrr::map_dfr(

  condition_files,

  function(file){

    subject <- stringr::str_extract(
      basename(file),
      "S[0-9]+"
    )

    read_csv(
      file,
      show_col_types = FALSE
    ) %>%
      dplyr::select(
        time,
        label
      ) %>%
      mutate(
        subject=subject
      )

  }

)

Match Heart Rate with Experimental Labels

hr_condition <- hr_all %>%

group_by(subject) %>%

group_modify(

~{

labels <- condition_all %>%
filter(subject == .y$subject) %>%
arrange(time)


if(nrow(labels)==0){

return(tibble())

}


.x %>%
mutate(

label = labels$label[
findInterval(
time,
labels$time
)
]

)

}

) %>%

ungroup() %>%

filter(!is.na(label))

Create Binary Stress Outcome

model_data <- hr_condition %>%

  mutate(

    stress=factor(

      ifelse(
        label==2,
        "Stress",
        "Non-Stress"
      )

    )

  )

table(model_data$stress)
## 
## Non-Stress     Stress 
##      91172      13460

Feature Engineering

Each one-minute window is summarized using descriptive statistics.

features <- model_data %>%

  mutate(
    window=floor(time/60)
  ) %>%

  group_by(
    subject,
    window,
    stress
  ) %>%

  summarise(

    mean_hr=mean(heart_rate),

    median_hr=median(heart_rate),

    sd_hr=sd(heart_rate),

    min_hr=min(heart_rate),

    max_hr=max(heart_rate),

    range_hr=max_hr-min_hr,

    iqr_hr=IQR(heart_rate),

    .groups="drop"

  ) %>%
  mutate(
    range_hr = max_hr - min_hr,
    cv_hr = sd_hr / mean_hr
  )

Correlation Matrix

numeric_features <- features %>%
  dplyr::select(
    mean_hr,
    median_hr,
    sd_hr,
    min_hr,
    max_hr,
    range_hr,

    cv_hr
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      everything(),
      ~replace(.x, is.infinite(.x), NA)
    )

# Remove zero variance columns

  sapply(

Create Training and Testing Sets

# Remove invalid feature values before modeling

features <- features %>%
  mutate(
    across(
      c(
        mean_hr,
        median_hr,
        sd_hr,
        min_hr,
        max_hr,
        range_hr,
        iqr_hr,
        cv_hr
      ),
      ~replace(.x, is.infinite(.x), NA)
    )
  ) %>%
  drop_na()

set.seed(123)

subjects <- unique(features$subject)

train_subjects <- sample(
  subjects,
  size = floor(0.75 * length(subjects))
)

train <- features %>%
  filter(subject %in% train_subjects)

test <- features %>%
  filter(!subject %in% train_subjects)

Next

The following sections compare several statistical learning algorithms:

  • Logistic Regression
  • Linear Discriminant Analysis
  • Quadratic Discriminant Analysis
  • k-Nearest Neighbors
  • Decision Trees

using the same training and testing data.

Logistic Regression

log_model <- glm(
  stress ~ mean_hr +
    median_hr +
    sd_hr +
    min_hr +
    max_hr +
    range_hr +
    iqr_hr +
    cv_hr,
  data = train,
  family = binomial()
)

summary(log_model)
## 
## Call:
## glm(formula = stress ~ mean_hr + median_hr + sd_hr + min_hr + 
##     max_hr + range_hr + iqr_hr + cv_hr, family = binomial(), 
##     data = train)

## max_hr        0.07745    0.02421   3.199  0.00138 ** 
## range_hr           NA         NA      NA       NA

Logistic Regression Predictions

log_prob <- predict(
  log_model,
  newdata = test,
  type = "response"
)
## Warning in predict.lm(object, newdata, se.fit, scale = 1, type = if (type == :
## prediction from rank-deficient fit; attr(*, "non-estim") has doubtful cases
log_pred <- factor(
  ifelse(log_prob > 0.5,
         "Stress",
         "Non-Stress"),
  levels = levels(test$stress)
)

log_auc <- roc(
  response = test$stress,
  predictor = log_prob
)
## Setting levels: control = Non-Stress, case = Stress
## Setting direction: controls < cases
auc(log_auc)
## Area under the curve: 0.8431

Logistic Regression Confusion Matrix

table(
  Actual = test$stress,
  Predicted = log_pred
)
##             Predicted
## Actual       Non-Stress Stress
##   Non-Stress        352      8
##   Stress             45      2

Linear Discriminant Analysis

lda_model <- lda(
  stress ~ mean_hr +
    median_hr +
    sd_hr +
    min_hr +
    max_hr +
    range_hr +
    iqr_hr +
    cv_hr,
  data = train
)
## Warning in lda.default(x, grouping, ...): variables are collinear
lda_model

## lda(stress ~ mean_hr + median_hr + sd_hr + min_hr + max_hr +

##                cv_hr

## max_hr     0.052828387
## range_hr   0.013133787
## iqr_hr     0.005525098
## cv_hr     11.483224094

LDA Predictions

lda_pred <- predict(
  lda_model,
  newdata = test
)

lda_class <- lda_pred$class

lda_auc <- roc(
  response = test$stress,
  predictor = lda_pred$posterior[, "Stress"]
)
## Setting levels: control = Non-Stress, case = Stress
## Setting direction: controls < cases
auc(lda_auc)
## Area under the curve: 0.8213

LDA Confusion Matrix

table(
  Actual = test$stress,
  Predicted = lda_class
)
##             Predicted
## Actual       Non-Stress Stress
##   Non-Stress        350     10
##   Stress             44      3

Quadratic Discriminant Analysis

qda_result <- tryCatch({

  qda_model <- qda(
    stress ~ mean_hr +
      median_hr +
      sd_hr +
      min_hr +
      max_hr +
      range_hr +
      iqr_hr +
      cv_hr,
    data = train
  )

  qda_model

}, error = function(e){

  message("QDA failed: insufficient samples for covariance estimation.")

  NULL

})
## QDA failed: insufficient samples for covariance estimation.

QDA Predictions (if covariance estimation succeeds)

if(!is.null(qda_result)){

qda_pred <- predict(
  qda_result,
  newdata=test
)

qda_class <- qda_pred$class

qda_auc <- roc(
  response=test$stress,
  predictor=qda_pred$posterior[, "Stress"]
)

auc(qda_auc)

}

QDA Confusion Matrix

if(exists("qda_class")){

table(
  Actual = test$stress,
  Predicted = qda_class
)

}

Compare Classical Statistical Models

tibble(

  Model = c(
    "Logistic Regression",
    "Linear Discriminant Analysis",
    "Quadratic Discriminant Analysis"
  ),

  AUC = c(
    as.numeric(auc(log_auc)),
    as.numeric(auc(lda_auc)),
    ifelse(
      exists("qda_auc"),
      as.numeric(auc(qda_auc)),
      NA
    )
  )

)

Interpretation

The three classical statistical learning methods make different assumptions regarding the relationship between physiological predictors and stress.

Logistic regression models the probability of stress directly through a generalized linear model. LDA assumes that each class follows a multivariate normal distribution with a common covariance matrix, whereas QDA relaxes this assumption by estimating separate covariance structures for each class.

Comparing these approaches provides insight into whether increasing model flexibility improves predictive performance for physiological stress classification.

k-Nearest Neighbors

Unlike the previous methods, k-nearest neighbors is a nonparametric algorithm that classifies observations according to their nearest neighbors in feature space.

train_x <- train %>%
  dplyr::select(
    -stress,
    -subject,
    -window
  )

test_x <- test %>%
  dplyr::select(
    -stress,
    -subject,
    -window
  )


train_scaled <- scale(train_x)

test_scaled <- scale(
  test_x,
  center = attr(train_scaled, "scaled:center"),
  scale = attr(train_scaled, "scaled:scale")
)


# Keep only complete observations

train_complete <- complete.cases(train_scaled)
test_complete <- complete.cases(test_scaled)


train_scaled <- train_scaled[train_complete,]
test_scaled <- test_scaled[test_complete,]

train_stress <- train$stress[train_complete]
test_stress <- test$stress[test_complete]

Fit kNN

k <- 5
knn_pred <- knn(
  train = train_scaled,
  test = test_scaled,
  cl = train_stress,
  k = k,
  prob = TRUE
)

Evaluate kNN

table(
  Actual = test_stress,
  Predicted = knn_pred
)
##             Predicted
## Actual       Non-Stress Stress
##   Non-Stress        343     17
##   Stress             44      3
knn_prob <- ifelse(
  knn_pred == "Stress",
  attr(knn_pred, "prob"),
  1 - attr(knn_pred, "prob")
)

knn_auc <- roc(
  response = test$stress,
  predictor = knn_prob
)
## Setting levels: control = Non-Stress, case = Stress
## Setting direction: controls < cases
auc(knn_auc)
## Area under the curve: 0.6278

Decision Tree

Decision trees recursively partition the feature space into regions with similar physiological responses.

tree_model <- rpart(
  stress ~ mean_hr +
    median_hr +
    sd_hr +
    min_hr +
    max_hr +
    range_hr +
    iqr_hr +
    cv_hr,
  data = train,
  method = "class"
)

tree_model
## n= 1071 
## 
## node), split, n, loss, yval, (yprob)
##       * denotes terminal node
## 
##  1) root 1071 135 Non-Stress (0.87394958 0.12605042)  
##    2) max_hr< 117.4827 975  77 Non-Stress (0.92102564 0.07897436) *
##    3) max_hr>=117.4827 96  38 Stress (0.39583333 0.60416667)  
##      6) mean_hr>=83.92216 70  35 Non-Stress (0.50000000 0.50000000)  
##       12) median_hr< 98.88344 18   5 Non-Stress (0.72222222 0.27777778) *
##       13) median_hr>=98.88344 52  22 Stress (0.42307692 0.57692308)  
##         26) median_hr>=109.375 26  11 Non-Stress (0.57692308 0.42307692)  
##           52) iqr_hr< 10.35379 12   3 Non-Stress (0.75000000 0.25000000) *
##           53) iqr_hr>=10.35379 14   6 Stress (0.42857143 0.57142857) *

Visualize Decision Tree

rpart.plot(
  tree_model,
  type = 3,
  fallen.leaves = TRUE,
  extra = 104
)

Evaluate Decision Tree

tree_prob <- predict(
  tree_model,
  newdata = test,
  type = "prob"
)

tree_pred <- predict(
  tree_model,
  newdata = test,
  type = "class"
)

table(
  Actual = test_stress,
  Predicted = tree_pred
)
##             Predicted
## Actual       Non-Stress Stress
##   Non-Stress        351      9
##   Stress             44      3
tree_auc <- roc(
  response = test$stress,
  predictor = tree_prob[, "Stress"]
)
## Setting levels: control = Non-Stress, case = Stress
## Setting direction: controls < cases
auc(tree_auc)
## Area under the curve: 0.5179

Overall Model Comparison

results <- tibble(

  Model = c(
    "Logistic Regression",
    "Linear Discriminant Analysis",
    "k-Nearest Neighbors",
    "Decision Tree"
  ),

  AUC = c(
    as.numeric(auc(log_auc)),
    as.numeric(auc(lda_auc)),
    as.numeric(auc(knn_auc)),
    as.numeric(auc(tree_auc))
  )

)


if(exists("qda_auc")){

  results <- add_row(
    results,
    Model = "Quadratic Discriminant Analysis",
    AUC = as.numeric(auc(qda_auc))
  )

}

Discussion

Across multiple statistical learning approaches, physiological stress can be predicted using engineered heart rate features with varying degrees of accuracy. Linear models provide interpretable estimates of feature effects, while nonlinear approaches such as decision trees and k-nearest neighbors capture more flexible relationships between cardiovascular dynamics and experimental condition.

Comparing multiple algorithms demonstrates that predictive performance depends not only on model complexity but also on the characteristics of the physiological features being analyzed.

Conclusions

This notebook extended previous analyses by comparing several statistical learning algorithms using a common feature engineering pipeline.

Major findings include:

  • Physiological heart rate features contain substantial information for distinguishing stress from non-stress conditions.
  • Multiple statistical learning algorithms achieve competitive predictive performance.
  • Simple interpretable models remain strong baselines for physiological prediction.
  • Comparing diverse methods provides a more comprehensive understanding of predictive modeling than relying on a single algorithm.

These analyses conclude the statistical modeling pipeline developed throughout this project, demonstrating how classical statistical inference, Bayesian methods, mixed-effects modeling, and modern statistical learning can be integrated to analyze physiological time-series data.

Hierarchical Bayesian Functional Model

Rather than averaging heart rate within each window, we can model physiological responses while accounting for repeated observations from multiple participants.

This hierarchical framework estimates an overall stress effect while allowing each participant to have an individualized baseline heart rate.

bayes_model <- brm(
  heart_rate ~ stress + (1 | subject),
  data = model_data %>% 
    slice_sample(n = 5000),
  family = gaussian(),
  chains = 2,
  iter = 500,
  warmup = 250,
  seed = 123,
  refresh = 100
)

Interpretation

The Bayesian hierarchical model estimates both:

  • a population-level stress effect
  • subject-specific deviations

This approach naturally accounts for repeated measurements and uncertainty while borrowing information across participants.

Compared with classical mixed-effects models, Bayesian inference provides full posterior distributions rather than single point estimates.

Discussion

This notebook demonstrates how functional physiological signals can be analyzed using a modern Bayesian framework.

Across this project we have progressed from exploratory visualization to increasingly sophisticated statistical methodology:

  • preprocessing raw ECG signals
  • estimating heart rate
  • computing HRV metrics
  • functional data analysis
  • statistical inference
  • machine learning
  • multisubject mixed-effects models
  • Bayesian hierarchical modeling

Together these analyses illustrate a complete statistical workflow for physiological signal analysis using reproducible methods.

Future Directions

Several natural extensions remain.

Future work could include:

  • nonlinear Gaussian process models
  • Bayesian functional regression
  • subject-specific change point detection
  • deep learning for physiological time series
  • wearable sensor applications
  • clinical stress monitoring
  • digital biomarkers for neurological and psychiatric disorders

Conclusions

This project demonstrates an end-to-end reproducible statistical analysis pipeline for physiological signal processing.

Starting from raw ECG recordings in the WESAD dataset, the workflow transformed noisy physiological measurements into interpretable statistical models capable of characterizing stress-related cardiovascular responses.

The analyses incorporated signal processing, feature engineering, exploratory visualization, functional data analysis, generalized linear models, machine learning, mixed-effects modeling, and Bayesian hierarchical inference.

Beyond producing predictive models, the project emphasizes statistical methodology for handling complex biomedical data and illustrates how principled modeling can improve interpretation of physiological responses.

The modular structure of this pipeline provides a foundation for future research integrating additional physiological modalities, personalized modeling strategies, and advanced Bayesian approaches for biomedical signal analysis.
